uncited: Progressive and Multi-stage Training refers to a family of optimization strategies that decompose the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations into sequential phases, rather than optimizing all parameters simultaneously from initialization.

By decoupling geometry initialization, appearance refinement, and high-frequency detail capture, these methods ensure that the Gaussian distribution adapts progressively to the scene's complexity [7173-hybrid-coarse-to-fine-strategy.md].

Unlike standard single-stage training, which often suffers from error propagation between pose and geometry or insufficient coverage of high-frequency details, multi-stage approaches isolate specific learning objectives (e.g., pose vs. attributes) to stabilize the optimization landscape [15018-multi-stage-training-with-pose-prediction.md].
All methods in this family operate on the Gaussian set $\mathcal{G}$ defined in [Densification Strategy](6234-densification-strategy.md).

The core mechanism involves partitioning the optimization timeline into distinct stages, where each stage modifies the set of trainable parameters, the supervision signals, and the densification triggers.

**Parameter Freezing/Unfreezing:** Stages typically freeze geometry-related parameters (positions, covariances, camera poses) while optimizing appearance parameters (SH coefficients, opacity), or vice versa, to prevent error propagation [15018-multi-stage-training-with-pose-prediction.md].

**Progressive Complexity:** Training often begins with simplified supervision signals (e.g., low-order SH, RGB-only, or coarse geometry) and gradually introduces higher complexity (e.g., high-order SH, perceptual losses, or dense densification) [7173-hybrid-coarse-to-fine-strategy.md, 17879-training-loop-with-mixed-losses-and-post-processing.md].
**Curriculum or Staged Supervision:** Different stages may use different data sampling strategies or loss functions.

For example, early stages might use slice-based supervision for local structure, while later stages use voxel-based supervision for global consistency [12921-curriculum-learning-with-slice-and-voxel-supervision.md].

**Densification Timing:** Densification (splitting/cloning) is often deferred or modified in early stages to establish a stable coarse topology before refining local details [7173-hybrid-coarse-to-fine-strategy.md, 22986-training-loop-with-structure-aware-densification.md].

- **Step:** Augment the initial model with larger sets of closer-up images (64 or 512 images) to simulate prolonged user interaction.
The concept of multi-stage training in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a response to the limitations of single-stage optimization, particularly in complex scenes or when dealing with sparse inputs.
Early implementations focused on coarse-to-fine strategies to stabilize geometry initialization [7173-hybrid-coarse-to-fine-strategy.md].

Subsequent work introduced pose-free training pipelines that decouple pose estimation from Gaussian attribute refinement to prevent error propagation [15018-multi-stage-training-with-pose-prediction.md].
Curriculum learning approaches were adapted from volumetric rendering to handle shear-warp pipelines [12921-curriculum-learning-with-slice-and-voxel-supervision.md].

More recent methods have integrated structure-aware densification and interleaved spatio-temporal updates to accelerate convergence and handle dynamic scenes [22986-training-loop-with-structure-aware-densification.md, S2].
These methods are widely used in novel view synthesis, 3D reconstruction from sparse views, and dynamic scene modeling.
